why: It gives the type's range and the large Tone boat's length, which set the frontage this page moors barges along; the 27 m Tone boat is the extreme of the type, an order above the 15-koku canal boat on the same page.

It gives the ward enclosed on all four sides with guarded gates shut at curfew, which is the sealed ward this page's fence stands for; a capital of the Tang, and it does not describe where a ward wall met the city wall, though it measures the wall-side streets that ran between the wards and the rampart; the walled, curfewed ward itself lapsed at the Tang-Song transition, so for a Ming-modeled seat it is an earlier form rather than a contemporary one. Its paragraph on the wards carries no reference of its own. It gives four gates only to a large ward; a small ward opened just two, east and west, so a fence drawn with four gates is the large-ward case.
It gives the round tower's resistance to sappers and projectiles and the square tower's vulnerable corners, which is Europe's reason this page sets beside the Song one.

It gives the European preference for round towers as deflecting shot, one half of the comparison this page makes; the reason it gives is the cannon-era one, later than the Song comparison this page draws and a different mechanism from the sapper-and-projectile reason.
It gives the gate as the point of controlled access for people, goods and animals and its uses for defense, trade and taxation, which is why this page clusters guard and inspection at the opening.
It states that a wall is crossed only at its gates and that works stopped traffic circumventing the city so that tolls were paid, which is the chokepoint this page's gate station rests on.

It gives the usual gate count by tier and what stood inside the wall, which sets this page's few grand gates; the tier gate counts (eight for a prefecture, four for a county) are an unreferenced generalization on the page, taken here for the shape and not the number.
It defines the tenement as standing on a back street or behind a merchant house and names its occupants, which is the lower-status housing this page lines its back lanes with.
It attests the market outside the wall and its descent from the rural periodic market, which is the gate market this page draws.

It gives the tower's height and bell and the one-tower-per-ten-blocks rule beside the block posts' ladders, which is the split between state and neighborhood watch; the one-tower-per-ten-blocks rule is the Kyōhō era's (1716-36) in the shogunal capital, not a general ratio.
It defines the precinct play, which is the stage this page gives a town; nothing on the stage's orientation.
It gives the gulf from the main-street house-owner to the back-street tenement dweller, which is the banding this page draws behind the road; no plan.

unsettled: The article is a terminology piece with no period attached and its ancestral-village case is the modern southern Chinese and Hong Kong walled village, so the table cannot place its evidence.

why: It gives the pack horse's load, 150 kin (about 90 kg) by a decree of 739 and 36 kan (about 135 kg) by the Edo regulation, both legal ceilings rather than measured loads, which is the ceiling this page puts on land carriage.
It defines the bund path, which is where this page has farmers walk past the field track's end; a dictionary line with no width.
It defines the porter's pole and its use to carry produce to market, which is the foot traffic this page pictures on a village lane; a stub that dates nothing.
It dates the boom to the Tenpo era and names the three great dojo of Edo, which is the late, urban institution this page keeps a dojo to.

It gives the city's million by 1721, the scale this page sets the great dojos in; it also states, in words and with no figure, that the townsmen's quarter was far more densely peopled than the samurai's, and that great lords' residences took dozens of hectares - Edo was the shogunal capital, so both ends of that contrast are larger than a provincial city's; the million is a historians' estimate, not a census; and when it was read the article carried two maintenance banners, one saying it lacks inline citations and one warning that it may include machine-generated text, so it is used for the direction of a contrast and never for a figure.

It gives the changeover on the fifth of the third and ninth months. The decree is the shogunate's for Edo, and the page's entries do not agree on when it took hold (the two cited works say 1668 or 1669, the Nipponica entry on the same page places it after the Meireki fire of 1657). It is not one fixed day: the older second and eighth months' changeover long coexisted with it, even in Edo, the date varied by region, and farm villages hiring servants by the year changed them over early in the twelfth month - so a village or hamlet map should not take the city date as its own.

It gives the provincial plot's enclosures - earthen wall, board fence or hedge - which is where this page's rank ladder takes its materials, though it attaches none of them to a rank; that a plot was granted by status and stipend, and changed with promotion; that a daimyo's Edo residence was ringed with row-house ranges for its retainers and servants while a smaller samurai house, with few live-in servants, had a wall instead; and that foot soldiers and the lowest retainers had no plot of their own but lived in shared row-houses, which the Nipponica places on the town's edge in many cases, not all, and whose size it says varied by domain. Without plans or counts; the Edo passages describe the shogun's capital, which the entry itself sets apart from the provincial castle town.

It defines the hall as in town, privately run and fee-paying and dates its flourishing to the Bakumatsu, which is the urban institution this page draws; the private and fee-paying definition is the modern trade's, with the Bakumatsu flourishing named as history.
It gives the yamen's jail and storehouses and the requirement that officials and clerks reside in it, which bears on this page's compound and on who was housed by the state; no plan.

It gives the scale a castle town's temple district could reach - some seventy temples close together in one of Kanazawa's three - which is the top of the range our temple quarters are measured against. Its limits are that Kanazawa was the seat of the largest domain in the country and one of its largest castle towns, so its temple stock is a ceiling and not a norm; and that it was three districts, not one.

It gives one dated case of a temple quarter made by a lord's decree - about twenty-five temples moved to ground west of the castle at Takada in 1614 - which sets the size of a castle town's temple quarter on our maps and the reading that it doubled as a defensive belt quartering foot soldiers. Its limits are that its count is hedged by its own writer ("probably about 25"); that it is one town in one province at one date, a point in a range and not a rule; and that the reading of "protection" as spiritual support plus billets for soldiers is the writer's interpretation, unattributed.

It gives a size-matched low anchor for a town's temple quarter - Takayama's, with more than ten temples and shrines - which bounds the bottom of the range our town maps draw. Its limits are that its count mixes Buddhist temples with Shinto shrines, so it is not a temple count; and that Takayama, its castle pulled down after 1692 and the town run from the intendancy office thereafter, is a particular kind of town.

We use it for the shape of a county seat's civic temple - not a single hall but a compound holding several cults side by side, the City God's own temple among them - which is how our town maps compose a precinct rather than dropping one building. The surviving buildings are later rebuildings of a much older foundation, and Pingyao was a wealthy town whose temple is a generous example rather than an average county one.

It carries in one sentence all three things this record asserts about monastic wealth - that manors were owned by monasteries among others, that they held oil mills, spinneries and breweries, and that the labor on them was slaves, craftsmen and tenant farmers - which is what puts productive enterprise inside a temple's economy on these maps rather than leaving a precinct as a place of worship only. Its limits are that its own authorities for this material, Gernet and Twitchett, could not be read.

We use it for the institutional facts behind a temple that lends - the monastery as the great pawnbroker, and pledged goods held in an associated warehouse or granary for the life of the loan - which is why a temple compound on our maps can reasonably carry a strongroom rather than only a hall. It is about China; we apply it to a Japanese-flavored setting on the strength of the monastic economy the two shared, not as a statement about any particular Japanese temple.

We use its statement that the earliest Chinese pawnbrokers were established and run by Buddhist monasteries, and its note that Southern Song laypeople formed partnerships with monasteries to open pawnshops, when deciding where a lending house belongs on a map - inside or beside a temple precinct rather than in a market row. China occupies a few sentences of a global survey, so we take the institutional association it describes and not a chronology or a count.

It is the statement behind this project’s householder clergy: a priest of the Zhengyi tradition marries, marriage is required at the highest rank, and the role is often passed down in a family - which is what puts families rather than celibates inside a temple precinct on these maps. Its limits are that it names no sources of its own.

We use it for one structural fact that shapes who lives beside a shrine on our maps - that the office was hereditary, held by a married priest whose children succeeded him, so a shrine implies a resident priestly household rather than a celibate community. Its most concrete statements are about the modern era, including the abolition of hereditary appointment in 1871, which is well after the period our setting is modeled on and which we use only as evidence of how deeply rooted the practice was before it.

It gives us what a rural temple contains as a domestic institution: a married clergy exempted by the Tokugawa government so a temple head could be married and still hold priestly status, a wife who runs the temple, and succession from father to eldest son - which is why our temple compounds carry a priest's family dwelling rather than a celibate dormitory. It describes one tradition, Jodo Shinshu, whose married clergy was the exception in the Edo period rather than the rule, so we use it for the shape of a temple household and not as a claim about every sect.

We use it for how timber reached a town, and it describes that chain in order: the loose-log drive handed off to rafts at the tying station, three men riding each raft, and the run down to the timber storage yard at Nagoya and the bay port beyond, which is what puts a log yard where we put it. It describes one valley's system, so the crew size and the yard locations are a worked example of how such a trade ran and not a national standard.

It gives the anatomy of the largest kind of boom - fixed cribs of stone-filled timber, the enclosure they make, the volume it held - from which the physics of anchoring and enclosure on our timber rivers is taken. Its limits are that it is industrial North America, not premodern East Asia, so the arrangement transfers and the scale does not; and that a lifetime total of logs is not on the page at all and is not used.

It gives the physical arrangement of a working boom - a river divided lengthwise, the logs held in pens along one side and a channel kept open beside them - which is why our timber-town booms run along a bank rather than across the river. Its limits are that it is industrial-era North America, where steam tugs, an army engineers' navigation channel and sawmill-scale volumes share the description with the physical arrangement, so the two have to be separated by hand and only the arrangement transfers; and that the navigation lawsuits it records are a modern American statutory and common-law regime with no premodern East Asian counterpart, so they explain that a boom must leave a channel, not who would have sued over it in our setting.

We use it for how a boom is built and held, which is what the log booms on our timber-town rivers are drawn from: a floating fence across a current, jointed so it rides the water, tied to solid ground at both banks. Its limits: it is about industrial-era logging in North America rather than East Asia, and its fittings - bolted timber groups, chains run over iron rollers - are nineteenth-century hardware a premodern river works would replace with lashings and rope, so what transfers is the principle of anchoring to fixed ground and not the fastenings; and the Hudson operation was far larger than anything at our settlements, so we take the arrangement from it and not the dimensions.

It gives the shape of a timber quarter - an off-river district of canals and storage ponds, logs kept afloat, rafts poled to the yards - which is what our timber towns' storage grounds are drawn from. Its limits are that much of its detail is twentieth-century, the Edo arrangement inferred from its survival and from the prints; and that Edo's timber quarter served the national market of the largest city in the country, so a provincial river town's timber ground is a scaled-down reading of it, not the same thing.

It gives a real case of a timber town made by its moorings - rafts along the bank, a market on the shore, a town behind it - which is the arrangement our river timber towns copy. Its limits are that it is one Chinese river port applied to our timber-town features; and that it carries no measurement of any kind, so a channel length is ours and unsourced.

We use it to keep two different river systems straight on a map, since a raft needs a wide steady channel and a landing where it can be broken up, while driving loose logs does not, and to keep raft sizes within a plausible order of magnitude. Its detailed dimensions come from European rivers such as the Rhine, so we treat them as the outer bound of what a raft can be rather than as a measurement of an East Asian one.

It gives the form of the gate range that fronts a samurai compound on our capital maps and the rank rule that governed who could build one, which is what makes the gate a marker of status a reader can read. Its limits are that it describes one domain's regulation and one surviving building from the very end of the period; and that it names only the servants' quarters and the stable as the range's contents - a gatekeeper's room, a storeroom and street-facing lookout windows are not on the page, so where our maps draw them they are a guess.

Very few sources put a measured plot size on the humblest warrior housing, and these give us both a size and the way enclosure rose with rank from hedge to fence to wall, which is what sets the fringe of our castle towns. It says plainly that Kaga's detached foot soldier houses were unusual for the period, most domains housing them in row tenements, so we treat these plots as one domain's practice that our maps may follow rather than a national norm.

It is a surviving building described by the people who keep it, which is why we use it for the nagayamon standing on the street and doubling as the quarters of the gatekeeper and the household servants, and for a room program that includes the servants' service rooms - both things our residence plans have to place. It is one house in one castle town. It is also not the house as first built: the main house was altered and extended several times after it was rebuilt in 1733, and the 2016-2019 conservation work restored it to a plan drawn in the Meiji period. So the room program shown is the house's late state, not a plan dated to the Edo period. The page names the service rooms (the miso room, the kitchen hearth, the bath) without saying who worked in them; that servants did is our reading. It tells us what one middle-rank residence in Matsue came to be, not what a typical residence anywhere was.

It is a local record of a surviving quarter that tells us the three things our layout needs: that the lowest-ranking retainers were housed on the outermost edge of the castle town as a defensive ring, the size of a single plot, and that men of one unit lived together along a numbered stretch of one street. It describes one domain - Hikone housed its ashigaru in detached houses with gardens where other domains used barrack rows, so the plot form is that domain's practice and not a national rule.

It is a surviving, officially documented building of exactly the type we draw for low-retainer housing, so it fixes the default terraced form and supplies real numbers for it: eight households in one range, about 18 ft of frontage each, roughly nine tsubo of floor apiece. Its limits are that it is one late-Edo building from one domain and that practice varied, since Kaga and Hikone housed their foot soldiers in detached houses with gardens, so the terrace is our default rather than a universal rule.

This is the source for the rule our samurai wards follow, that rank sets distance from the castle and that ranks of small uniform housing belong on the outer fringe of the ward. That is a rule at the scale of the town: at the scale of one compound the article itself records row houses (nagaya) within daimyo households, at home and in Edo, and nagaya gates at senior retainers' houses, so it does not rule nagaya out of a great house's fence. It gives no plot dimensions, setbacks or counts, so it decides the pattern while the measurements come from elsewhere, and it describes the Edo-period castle town specifically rather than samurai housing in every era. Its section on retainers' houses (侍屋敷) carries a banner (May 2025) saying it cites no sources, and that section is where the finer gradient lives: that rank falls step by step with distance from the lord's seat, that ashigaru housing massed at the town's entrances for defense, where karo lived, and that senior houses had a shikidai. Only the lead's sentence, upper samurai inside the middle moat and ashigaru row houses outside them, is cited, to a page of Japan's National Institute for Land and Infrastructure Management (国土技術政策総合研究所), the closer source for that pattern.

It gives the plan of a real county yamen in the words of a reporter walking it - the central axis, the two front courtyards, the Six Chambers, the total area and room count, and what stood east and west of the first court - which is what our magistracy plan is laid out from. Its limits are that the buildings are a late-Qing rebuild conserved and restored as a museum, so the plan is a preserved one rather than a documented original; that its west line holds the guest hall, the dining hall and the jail, not a clerks' lodging, and it names no sheds against the wall - the record uses Neixiang as the counter-example on both, and the runners' duty courtyard it does name stands on the east; and that it is imperial China rather than Japan.

A modest domain's castle is the right anchor for a typical capital, and it makes the point a reader most often gets wrong: the tower is a small part of the castle, not the castle itself. What it measures is the surviving park as it stands today, so its dimensions approximate the historical footprint rather than survey it. The hectare figures our castle sizing rests on (about 50 ha with the moats, a keep under one) are not on this page: they came from the park's own site, which we have not been able to cite, so they stand as a guess checked against the 612 by 947 m outline the article does give.

These are the numbers that fix the grand end of our castle range, and the moat widths in particular set how broad a defensive water line should read on a map. Himeji is exceptional rather than typical, so it is an upper bound and never a median, and its measurements are of the modern site as preserved and restored, including ground whose Edo-period use is no longer visible.

That census line is our population anchor for a domain capital - it shows what a substantial domain's town actually held in commoners, and, with the exemption noted, why the samurai population has to be estimated separately rather than read off. It describes a single town in a single domain, which we treat as one point on a range and not as a standard.

It is an attested Japanese case of a castle taking a river branch as the moat on two of its flanks, which is the thing our river city and edge castle maps need a real example for. It is a site's own account, so we use it for the fact and the shape of the river diversion and would not press it for dimensions, dates or anything finer than it plainly states.

It answers a layout question for a capital map: the bureaucracy sits on the ceremonial avenue outside the palace wall rather than inside it, which decides where the ministry compounds are drawn. Two limits are worth stating plainly - that particular sentence is flagged in the article as lacking a citation, so we treat the arrangement as a plausible shape to draw rather than as a documented fact; and Ming and Qing Beijing is a Chinese imperial capital standing in for our setting's own, which is modeled on both China and Japan.

It gives the arrangement our castle plans follow: the palace at the core as both residence and the working seat of domain government, the keep a separate defensive tower, and the third bailey given over to the mansions of the senior retainers. Its limits are that Nagoya was one of the largest castles in the country, so it stands for the arrangement of a castle's parts and never for their size at a provincial seat.

It gives one Edo-period case of a castle's inner enclosure proving too small for its government: after the 1727 fire the functions moved to the second bailey, and because that was smaller the county office, the town office and the hall where the lord met the village headmen were moved out into the town - the warrant for putting some of a castle town's official buildings outside the walls on our maps. Its limits are that it is a single case; and that its dates want care, since the page carries at least one internal error in them.

It is directly about the feature we draw - a fence closing a street at night - and it supplies the reason such a fence existed, which is the curfew that a city's night watch enforced. Its limits are that Beijing is an imperial capital and so the strictest case of urban policing in the empire: a provincial town would have had a looser version of the same arrangement, and the specific curfew hours and lash counts come from separate reporting rather than from this paper.

It tells us that the daimyo's warehouse-residences stood at the market, in the commercial capital where the rice was sold, rather than at the domain seat - which is why our capitals do not carry rows of them. Its limits are that it describes one exceptional city at the peak of one trade; that the key bundles two other works that are neither linked nor quoted, so nothing readable rests on them; and that the figure of more than a hundred such houses at the early-1800s peak is not in the passage we quote, so it stands as a guess until a page carries it.

It gives the form of the towpath - a real riverside way, and the slab-on-piers kind standing just above the water - which is what a towpath on our canal maps is drawn from. Its limits are that it describes a preserved heritage structure as it stands now, whose fabric is later than the institution; that the date, the length and the Marco Polo detail are not on the page and rest on nothing readable, so they stand as guesses; and that a Chinese canal stands in for a setting whose surface is often Japanese.
